Elastic Functional Bayesian Model Calibration¶

Example notebook demonstrating workflow for EFBMC. We will demonstrate this method calibrating a simulated data set

Code locations are availble below:

  1. impala
  2. fdasrvf
  3. mvBayes
  4. pyBASS

Other surrogate models:

  1. pyBayesPPR
  2. stochtree

First we need to import the required packages

In [3]:
import numpy as np
import os
from impala import superCal as sc
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.cm as cm
import pyBASS as pb
import mvBayes as mb
import fdasrsf as fs
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd
import arviz as az
from scipy.stats import norm
from scipy.interpolate import Akima1DInterpolator

Data Pre-processing¶

We will simulate a simple toy data set with parameters

In [4]:
def f(x):
    out = norm.pdf(tt, np.sin(2 * np.pi * x[0] ** 2) / 4 - x[0] / 10 + 0.55, 0.05) * x[1]
    # out = norm.pdf(tt, x[0]+.01, 0.05) * x[1]
    return out

M = 99
tt = np.linspace(0, 1, M)
n = 100
p = 3
x_train = np.random.rand(n, p)
x_test = np.random.rand(1000, p)
e = np.random.normal(size=n * M)
y_train = (
    np.apply_along_axis(f, 1, x_train) + e.reshape(n, M) * 0
)  # with higher error, smooth first
y_test = np.apply_along_axis(f, 1, x_test)

Next we will generate the observation (experiment)

In [5]:
x_true = np.array([0.1028, 0.5930])
# x_true = [.3,.2]
f_obs = f(x_true)
y_obs = f_obs + np.random.normal(size=M) * 0.05

Look at the original data with the experiment overlaid

In [6]:
plt.plot(tt, y_train.T, color='lightgrey')
plt.plot(tt, y_obs, color='black') 
plt.legend(['model runs','experiment'])
ax = plt.gca()
leg = ax.get_legend()
leg.legend_handles[0].set_color('lightgrey')
leg.legend_handles[1].set_color('black');

Elastic Functional Alignment¶

We will now align the computer model output to the experiment. We will need the aligned data ftilde_train and the shooting vectors vv_train. Additionally we will need the shooting vector for the experiment. In this case, since we are aligning to the experiment warping function will be identity ($\gamma_{id}$) and then the corresponding shooting vector vv_obs.

There is the option of the parameter lam in multiple_align_functions that restricts the amount of alignment. In some cases we will set this to a small value (e.g., 0.01) to remove heteroskedacity from the warping functions.

In [7]:
tt = np.linspace(0,1,M)
out = fs.fdawarp(y_train.T, tt)
out.multiple_align_functions(y_obs, parallel=True, lam=0.01)
gam_train = out.gam
vv_train = fs.geometry.gam_to_psi(gam_train)
ftilde_train = out.fn
qtilde_train = out.qn

gam_obs = np.linspace(0, 1, M)
vv_obs = fs.geometry.gam_to_psi(gam_obs)

We will now plot the alignment results. First is the aligned functions.

In [8]:
plt.plot(tt, ftilde_train, color='lightgrey')
plt.plot(tt, y_obs, color='black') 
plt.legend(['model runs','experiment'])
ax = plt.gca()
leg = ax.get_legend()
leg.legend_handles[0].set_color('lightgrey')
leg.legend_handles[1].set_color('black');

Then the corresponding warping functions

plt.plot(tt, gam_train, color='lightgrey')
plt.plot(tt, gam_obs, color='black') 
plt.legend(['model runs','experiment'])
ax = plt.gca()
leg = ax.get_legend()
leg.legend_handles[0].set_color('lightgrey')
leg.legend_handles[1].set_color('black');

and the corresponding shooting vectors

In [10]:

plt.plot(tt, vv_obs, color='black') 
plt.legend(['model runs','experiment'])
ax = plt.gca()

Surrogate Model Fitting¶

Next, we will fit the BASS surrogate to the computer model and evaluate its performance. We use the mvBayes package due to its ability to introspect surrogates and their performance.

The choice of nBasis here is made from exploratory data analysis. It can also be chosen based on the percentage of variance explained from the functional principal component analysis (fPCA) decomposition. The parameter in mvBayes do perform this is propVarExplained.

The parameter idxSamplesArg sets which parameter the emulator (BASS) uses to pick mcmc samples for prediction. In this case the parameter is mcmc_use.

We also optional tell mvBayes to extract the residual standard deviation from the s2 samples since BASS provides it. If the chosen emulator does not provide, mvBayes will estimate it.

In [11]:
emu_ftilde = mb.mvBayes(pb.bass, 
                        x_train, 
                        ftilde_train.T, 
                        idxSamplesArg='mcmc_use',
                        # optionally extract posterior samples of residual standard deviation
                        residSDExtract = lambda bass_out: np.sqrt(bass_out.samples.s2) )

emu_vv = mb.mvBayes(pb.bass, 
                    x_train, 
                    vv_train.T, 
                    basisType="pns",
                    idxSamplesArg='mcmc_use',
                    # optionally extract posterior samples of residual standard deviation
                    residSDExtract = lambda bass_out: np.sqrt(bass_out.samples.s2) )

We can examine the fit of the surrogate model by looking at mvBayes diagnostic plots. We want to examine the MSE and if it is reasonable as well as the $R^2$ value to make sure its high enough. Also we can use the lower right panel to see how much explained variance is contained in the 7 principal components.

In [12]:
emu_ftilde.plot()

We can also examine the fPCA decomposition to explore it more further if needed. We see that 7 components contain 99% of the explained variance

In [13]:
emu_ftilde.basisInfo.plot()

Lets evaluate the shooting vector emulator

In [14]:
emu_vv.plot()

Bayesian Model Calibration¶

We will now set up impala to perform the calibration. First we need to setup the parameter names and bounds on the parameters. impala sets uniform priors on the parameters based on their bounds.

In [15]:
input_names = ['X1','X2','X3']
bounds_mat = np.array([[x_train[:,i].min(), x_train[:,i].max()] for i in range(p)])
bounds = dict(zip(input_names, bounds_mat))

We will now set up the calibration object and add the experimental data for the aligned data and shooting vectors. impala is set up to run multiple chains and do annealing so we set up a temperature ladder of 20 chains. We also set the chains to run for 4000 samples with a burn in of 2000 samples. The last line runs the calibration.

In [16]:
setup = sc.CalibSetup(bounds, constraint_func="bounds")
model_ftilde = sc.ModelmvBayes(emu_ftilde, input_names) # for aligned data
model_vv = sc.ModelmvBayes(emu_vv, input_names) # for warping functions
setup.addVecExperiments(y_obs, 
    model_ftilde, 
    sd_est=np.array([0.001]), 
    s2_df=np.array([20.]), 
    s2_ind=np.array([0]*M))
setup.addVecExperiments(vv_obs, 
    model_vv, 
    sd_est=np.array([0.1]), 
    s2_df=np.array([20.]), 
    s2_ind=np.array([0]*M))
setup.setTemperatureLadder(1.05**np.arange(20))
setup.setMCMC(10000,2000,1,10)
out = sc.calibPool(setup)

[2026-04-28 15:12:20 | 9999/9999 (100%) | WALL: 0:02:56 | ETA: 0:00:00 | 56.73it/s]
Calibration MCMC Complete. Time: 176.268775 seconds.

Next we will extract the parameters for the last 2000 samples and thin by 1.

In [17]:
uu = np.arange(8000, 10000, 2)

theta_dict = sc.tran_unif(out.theta[uu,0,:], setup.bounds_mat, setup.bounds.keys())
ftilde_pred_obs = setup.models[0].eval(theta_dict)
vv_pred_obs = setup.models[1].eval(theta_dict)
gam_pred_obs = fs.geometry.psi_to_gam(vv_pred_obs.T)

Now we will look at the likelihood and chains to make sure the MCMC chains are stable and have converged.

In [18]:
plt.plot(out.llik)
plt.title('Log Likelihood')

nplots = len(input_names)
ns1 = int(np.ceil(np.sqrt(nplots)))
ns2 = int(np.round(np.sqrt(nplots)))
fig, axs = plt.subplots(ns1, ns2)
for i, ax in enumerate(fig.axes):
    if i < nplots:
        ax.plot(out.theta_native[input_names[i]])
        ax.set(title=input_names[i])
plt.tight_layout()

Examine the pair plot of the parameters. The diagonal contains the posterior distributions of the parameters. The off diagonal is the dependence. The dots are colored by how they appear in the chain (blue is early and red is late). This also helps determine if the chains are mixing well.

In [22]:
dat = pd.DataFrame(out.theta_native)
dat = dat[input_names]
dat = dat.loc[uu,:]
dat.insert(0,'idx',dat.index,allow_duplicates = False)
g = sns.PairGrid(dat.loc[:, dat.columns != 'idx'], diag_sharey=False);
g.map_upper(sns.scatterplot, palette = 'coolwarm', hue=dat['idx'], legend=False);
g.map_lower(sns.kdeplot, cmap="viridis", fill=True, thresh=0.05);
g.map_diag(sns.histplot, kde=True);

Next we are going to evaluate the surrogate model at the calibrate parameters for the entire posterior distribution. They gray curves are the computer model, blue curves are the calibrated surrogate curves, and black is the experiment.

In [23]:
plt.figure()
plt.plot(tt, ftilde_train, color="lightgrey")
plt.plot(tt, ftilde_pred_obs.T, color="lightblue")
plt.plot(tt, y_obs, color="black")
plt.title('Aligned Functions')

plt.figure()
plt.plot(tt, vv_train, color="lightgrey")
plt.plot(tt, vv_pred_obs.T, color="lightblue")
plt.plot(tt, vv_obs, color="black")
plt.title('Shooting Vectors')

plt.figure()
plt.plot(tt, gam_train, color="lightgrey")
plt.plot(tt, gam_pred_obs, color="lightblue")
plt.plot(tt, gam_obs, color="black")
plt.title('Warping Vectors')

We then combine the outputs of the emulators via composition to look at in the original data space

In [24]:
obspred_all = np.zeros([len(uu), M])
for i in range(len(uu)):
    obspred_all[i, :] = fs.warp_f_gamma(
        tt, ftilde_pred_obs[i, :], fs.invertGamma(gam_pred_obs[:, i])
    )

plt.plot(tt, y_train.T, color="lightgrey")
plt.plot(tt, obspred_all.T, color="lightblue")
plt.plot(tt, y_obs, color="black")
plt.title("Original Data Prediction")
plt.legend(["model runs", "calibrated predictions", "experiment"])
ax = plt.gca()
leg = ax.get_legend()
leg.legend_handles[0].set_color("lightgrey")
leg.legend_handles[1].set_color("lightblue")
leg.legend_handles[2].set_color("black")

Sensitivity Analysis¶

We can also perform sensitivity analysis on the surrogate through mvBayes by doing the following. The BASS emulator has a closed form sobol indices and we will utilize that. mvBayes also provides the ability to monte carlo to determine the sobol indices.

First we will look at the amplitude surrogate

In [25]:
emu_ftilde.mvSobol(idxSamplesArg='mcmc_use') # 'mcmc_use' is bppr's equivalent of idxSamples
emu_ftilde.plotSobol(labels=input_names)

Start

Next the phase surrogate

In [26]:
emu_vv.mvSobol(idxSamplesArg='mcmc_use') # 'mcmc_use' is bppr's equivalent of idxSamples
emu_vv.plotSobol(labels=input_names)
